title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline under a frozen protocol that used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM candidate generated per intent and replayed to both arms). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was not exercised, the experiment does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations; its empirical contribution is a deterministic, preregistered accounting and a set of artifact-grounded design lessons (generation semantics, adversary potency, verifier strength, and budgeting) to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises well-founded concerns about security-relevant misconfigurations that can increase attack surface or violate access-control policies. Prior surveys and systems work therefore recommend integrating execution oracles, constrained generation, human oversight, or iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as operational mitigations [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. However, rigorous preregistered confirmatory evidence that a verifier placed in the loop reliably reduces forbidden-reachability misconfigurations under adversarial inputs is limited.

We asked a narrowly scoped operational question and fixed it before execution: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? To answer this we preregistered a paired binary experiment (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) with N = 300 matched intents and deterministic validators, executed the plan under a frozen adapter contract, and archived all per-episode traces, provider-call audits, and analysis outputs.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered, deterministic paired execution with full per-episode validator traces and provider-call accounting for N = 300 matched intents. (2) A concise, artifact-grounded technical definition of the forbidden-reachability predicate and a summary of the deterministic validators used. (3) Confirmatory empirical outcomes and exact inferential statistics: n11 = 300, McNemar p = 1.0, bootstrap CI = [0.0,0.0], Clopper–Pearson upper bound ≈ 0.00994. (4) Evidence-grounded design lessons and reproducibility materials to guide follow-up stress tests that exercise the GVR repair path (independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, larger repair budgets, and richer oracles). Importantly, because no repair was invoked, the run cannot demonstrate that verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs; we make that limitation explicit.
sections.related_work:
Three strands of prior work informed our design. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness for code and Infrastructure-as-Code by using execution or verifier feedback to direct repairs; system papers emphasize that verifier power and repair strategy determine realized gains [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W7124141852]. Second, surveys and NetOps-focused reviews document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch—and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Third, emulation and testbed studies show that execution-based validation is practical for research evaluations but warn about external-validity gaps when transporting results to production devices and live traffic [https://openalex.org/W4406170828].

These literatures motivate verifier-in-the-loop architectures but leave open the question of whether a preregistered, paired, execution-accountable experiment can demonstrate repair efficacy under adversarial prompts. Our study targets that specific gap by preregistering estimands, execution semantics, and deterministic validators, and by archiving exhaustive per-episode traces to permit audit and follow-up stress tests.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. We preregistered a paired binary design (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1): N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). Primary test: exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). Prespecified CIs: bootstrap-percentile; final analysis used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration fixed sampling, deduplication, exclusion rules, and sensitivity analyses (technical failures treated as violations in one sensitivity plan). All elements were archived prior to execution.

Adapter contract and generation semantics. To limit provider usage the execution contract used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each pair we generated a single LLM candidate and replayed that identical candidate to both arms (baseline and guarded). This produced model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs; the contract allowed up to 600 calls but conserved budget by sharing the initial generation. Crucially, shared replay means baseline is not an independent-generation arm; this reduces between-arm sampling variance and the chance of observing discordant violating outputs across the pair. We preregistered this choice and its trade-offs.

Intervention arms and repair policy. Baseline: replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded: the same initial candidate validated by the deterministic validators; if any validator reported forbidden reachability the protocol allowed up to one repair LLM call (max one repair per pair). The repair prompt template and invocation rule were frozen in the transformation manifest. Across the run no repair prompts were issued because validators never flagged forbidden reachability.

Forbidden-reachability predicate and validators (technical definition). The forbidden-reachability predicate used in per-episode scoring flags configurations that introduce reachability from previously disallowed source–destination classes to protected resources or interfaces defined by the task payload (for example protected_interfaces = ["mgmt1"] and group constraints captured in the task manifest). Operationally, a configuration is labeled violating if it enables at least one previously-forbidden end-to-end forwarding relation that would allow packets from an untrusted or external interface class to reach a protected interface or otherwise violate task-provided access constraints. To detect this predicate we used two deterministic validators: (1) a containerized execution-style validator (Batfish-like) that executes parsed config changes against the emulated control/data plane to observe reachability outcomes, and (2) a lightweight static graph-based reachability analyzer implemented in Python that reasons over normalized device-state graphs. Both validators are deterministic in the emulated environment; their outputs were combined with a logical-OR decision rule (a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports forbidden reachability). Per-episode validator traces and the validator identifiers (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0') are archived for reproducibility and independent assessment of false-negative risk.

Emulator, tasks, and determinism. The environment used Dockerized FRRouting-style router images and deterministic orchestration; initial and expected final states, workflow policies (protected_interfaces, must_be_down_for_fields, group constraints) and difficulty metadata were encoded per task in the task manifest. Task generation applied deterministic seeds and programmatic adversarial perturbations (one adversarial variant per benign seed) with exact-duplicate and fuzzy-deduplication checks preregistered and executed.

Analysis plan. Primary inference used exact McNemar two-sided on complete matched pairs. We computed 95% bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Sensitivity analyses planned to treat technical/model failures as violations; no technical failures occurred. All raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audits, and analysis logs were archived as the reproducibility backbone.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The adapter completed planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms) with completed = 600 and failed episodes = 0. Provider-call accounting under shared_initial_candidate semantics recorded model_calls_used = 300 (stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Representative per-episode artifacts show the shared-candidate playback and the validator traces used for scoring.

Primary confirmatory outcome. Every paired intent passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided test p = 1.0. The prespecified bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the paired risk-difference is [0.0, 0.0]. Because no initial candidate triggered a validator-detected forbidden reachability the preregistered repair path was never invoked (all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false). Verifier concordance in the archived traces is perfect for this run (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0).

Descriptive bounding. Observing 0/300 violations provides a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994. We report this numeric bound as a descriptive constraint on undetected baseline violations under the exact contract (model, validators, emulator, and task set used).

Representative examples. Representative task artifacts show typical medium- and hard-difficulty workflows (shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change); in each archived example the shared initial candidate matched the expected normalized configuration and validators reported no violations. All per-episode raw responses, parser-normalized configurations, and validator judgments are archived to enable independent spot-checking.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and what the evidence supports. Under the exact experimental contract (declared model: gpt-5-mini; shared_initial_candidate generation; two deterministic validators combined by logical OR; Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; programmatic adversarial variants used here) baseline generation already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every sampled intent; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archived provider-call audit, per-episode validator_trace entries, and the paired contingency are consistent and deterministic.

Why the confirmatory hypothesis was untestable here. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis intended to test whether a verifier-in-the-loop reduces security-increasing misconfigurations via repair. Two coupled, preregistered design outcomes rendered that hypothesis untestable in this run: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical initial candidates in both arms and therefore reduced between-arm sampling variance (baseline was a replay, not an independent draw); and (2) none of the initial candidates triggered validator-detectable forbidden reachability. With zero discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) the McNemar paired test cannot evaluate repair efficacy. We state this explicitly so readers do not misinterpret the null paired difference as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in general.

Design lessons and operational recommendations (artifact-grounded). (A) Generation semantics matter: shared replay conserves provider budget (model_calls_used = 300) but reduces independent-sample variability needed to generate discordant violations that repairs could correct. For experiments aiming to exercise repair efficacy, use independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or increase repair-call budgets; the execution manifest quantifies the provider-call budget trade-off. (B) Adversary potency matters: the programmatic adversarial variants used here did not produce validator-detectable violations for the selected model and validators; stronger or targeted adversaries (or adversary-in-the-loop attack generators) are necessary to stress repair. (C) Verifier diversity and strength matter: two deterministic validators with logical OR were sufficient to detect nothing in this configuration; richer oracles and production-grade execution validators should be included in follow-ups. (D) Reproducibility and auditability are practical: the archived per-episode traces, provider-call audit, and analysis logs enable deterministic replay of the accounting and contingency outcomes.

Threats to validity (artifact-referenced). Internal validity is constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope (execution/model_configuration.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json show single-model runs and shared generation). Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately capture operational security risk; validator identifiers and per-episode traces are archived to support independent assessment. External validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and executed in Dockerized emulation; results may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic. Conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and preregistered power assumptions (nonzero baseline violation rate) are unmet. We preserve these artifacts to allow targeted reanalysis and follow-up experiments designed to exercise the repair path.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and deterministically executed a paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation (declared LLM: gpt-5-mini; N = 300 matched intents). The run completed as planned with model_calls_used = 300 under a shared_initial_candidate contract and produced a degenerate confirmatory outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate for all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never flagged violations, the repair path was not invoked and the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating outputs. The primary empirical contributions are the preregistered design, deterministic execution accounting, and comprehensive archived per-episode traces that demonstrate how generation semantics, adversary potency, verifier strength, and budget choices determine whether a follow-up experiment can exercise repair. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to support reproducible follow-up stress tests with independent condition generation, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; preregistered power assumptions (target 30 percentage-point absolute reduction) are unmet.

GVR not exercised: validators never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the preregistered repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant under the chosen contract, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; independent-condition generation or larger repair-call budgets would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation scope: the programmatic adversarial variants used here (one deterministic variant per benign seed) did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for this model and validator configuration; stronger, targeted, or adaptive adversaries are required to stress verifier and repair behavior.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic, or operator-in-the-loop workflows.

Model and verifier scope: evaluation used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators combined by logical OR; other LLMs, richer verifiers, or ensembles may produce different detection and repair dynamics.
